en: *Qixin zashuo* (Miscellaneous Discourses on Arousing Faith), compiled by Zhou Anshi (名思仁) of Lucheng,
based on the teachings of the Pure Land. It states that it is very easy to exhort those of great wisdom to convert and guide others, because their past merit is profound.
Hou’s capacity was no ordinary one. To exhort common men and women through the teachings of the Pure Land was easy to transform and guide, for they lacked preconceived notions;
it was like sweet nectar that can accept seasoning, or white silk that can receive dye.
Yet, to communicate these teachings to us, the literati who have studied the classics, was quite another matter indeed. This is because...
Formerly, there was a certain kind of antiquated attachment firmly rooted in their hearts;
thus, even when the Ultimate Way was present, they were unwilling to hear it, and even when there were excellent words, they were unwilling to listen.

Therefore, I have compiled several excerpts of words that point the way to guidance and inspire faith, which can be used to illuminate the Pure Land teachings, to serve as a source of Dharma-joy. This is titled:
*Qixin zashuo* (Miscellaneous Discourses on Arousing Faith). Table of Contents for *Qixin zashuo*:
Layman Yan Bing of Ruru encourages the practice of cultivation; the obstacles of principle and phenomena are even more severe than those of desire.
First, one must understand the doctrine of the three periods of time and further clarify the principle of cause and effect.

Regarding the principle of the three periods, Confucius must have certainly spoken of it; therefore, the wise should not regard themselves as short-lived, and those with wisdom must not narrow their scope of learning and experience. One must not fail to read the Tripitaka.
Master Xuanzang was skilled at inspiring [others]; he should have developed a sense of weary detachment toward his physical body.
A person of great filial piety does not wish to enter a womb; a person of high status must know how to feel self-reproach.
This is illustrated by the metaphors of the silkworm’s cocoon and the fish-trap basket.
The Simile of the Horse; the Simile of the Wild Fox;
Blaming the Lord of Death; the Moth that Flies into the Lamp;
the Fly in the Window; and the Four Methods for Training a Horse.
If one has made a vow for the eye-medicine to fulfill one's wishes, and if one has become a monk, one must not fail to cultivate the Pure Land. Even eminent monks should cultivate the Pure Land;
they must not be content to become ghosts. All nine classes of beings should attain rebirth there.
The method for practicing mindfulness of the Buddha without fail is that among all human affairs, none is superior to mindfulness of the Buddha.
This is the Exhortation to Practice by the Layman Yan Bing, known as Ruru:
"Everyone cherishes this physical body, yet who believes that the body is the root of suffering? Moment by moment, people greedily pursue pleasure, unaware [of its true nature]."
Pleasure is the cause of suffering. This fleeting life is easily passed; how could one dwell in it for long? This illusory body is not solid; it all returns to extinction.
Those who live long reach only eighty or ninety before they perish; those with short lives do not survive beyond two or three decades before they die prematurely.
Furthermore, there is today but no knowledge of what tomorrow may bring. Again, one may suddenly part from those on the bed as soon as one steps off the mat with their shoes.
How many are gone in a single breath, only to be parted forever for a thousand autumns? To lament that this body has no permanence is the truth;
yet alas, who among people is not deceived by it? Seven feet of bone wrapped in sinew, a lump of flesh covered in skin, hair, fur, nails, and teeth.
Fluids flow like heaps of dust; tears, phlegm, and saliva defile it like a moving latrine. In winter’s cold and summer’s heat, one steals a living year after year amidst malarial fevers.
Bitten by lice and pierced by mosquitoes, one passes age after age in confusion among maggots.
This body is not to be cherished; all you people should vow to transcend it. How can those who are deluded and ignorant still flaunt their "refinement"? You dull-witted fellows!
They still give rise to inverted views. Some pin flowers or grass upon their skulls; others carry musk or incense at the side of their stinking skin-sacks.
Fine silken robes completely cover bags of pus and blood, while brocade quilts entirely conceal buckets of excrement and urine.

They exhaust every deceitful mind and hundredfold schemes, imagining they shall dwell in this world for ten thousand years, unaware that their heads ache and their eyes grow dim. Then King Yama receives them.
When people arrive at this state—hair streaked with gray and teeth fallen out—the Ghost of Impermanence sends its message seeking them.

Each person clings to beauty and covets wealth; these are all swift paths to losing one's human form. Day after day they indulge in wine and relish meat; these are nothing but the planting of deep roots for the hells.
They strive for fleeting pleasure before their eyes, only to suffer bitter agony for ten thousand kalpas thereafter. Once the life-root [is severed]...
At this point of extremity, when the four great winds and knives cut you, externally your limbs and hands are pulled and stretched, while internally your liver and intestines tear with pain.
Even if your wife and children cherish you, there is no way to keep you; even if your own flesh and blood fill your presence, who could take your place?
The living lament in vain with piercing grief; the dead merely perceive their consciousness rushing forward. Seeing no light ahead, they find themselves utterly without companions.
Upon crossing the banks of the Nai River, there is none who does not feel sorrow; upon entering the Pass of the Ghost Gate, all who arrive naturally fall into desolation.
Only seven days having passed since their departure from the world, they cast themselves into the underworld and gradually pass through its various offices.
The officials of the court clutch their ledgers, devoid of human feeling; the jailers hold their pitchforks, their faces never smiling.

Those who practiced virtue throughout their lives are sent back to the Path of the Gods, the Path of the Immortals, and the Path of Humans. Those who committed evil during their days are driven into the Cauldron of Boiling Water, the Cauldron of Fire, and the Cauldron of Blades.
At first, everyone said that cause and effect were absurd; only now do we know that these words are not false. Within the mirror of retribution, every detail is laid bare;
within the dark realm of the dead, there is suffering at every turn. On the mountains of knives and trees of swords, one endures ten thousand kinds of torment;
as horned beasts and hairy creatures, one cannot repay the karmic debts of many lifetimes. No matter how bold your heart or how reckless your spirit may be, you shall not escape.
One may bow one's head before the ghost-wardens and rely on them to slander the Way and disparage the Sangha; yet when the time comes to face King Yama, one cannot help but kneel in submission.
Though the soul has returned to the realm of the dead, the physical corpse still lies within the coffin. It may be three or five days since its passing.
In the sixth or seventh month, it will rot and produce worms and blood; its foul stench will permeate both the earth and the heavens.
Those without wealth or status will be consigned to a heap of wild fire; those with dignity and face will be buried in desolate mountains thousands of li away.
That once lovely and rosy countenance has turned to ashes today; these desolate white bones have changed into dust.
Former loves and attachments have become empty here; where are the heroes of old now? By the green grass lie idle tombstones;
within the green willows hang empty paper offerings. When one thinks of the final conclusion at the end of life, who can escape it?
It is thus. If you wish to leap out of saṃsāra, you must turn your heart toward perfect enlightenment. Cease seeking a livelihood within the ghost cave;
you must know that the True Person resides upon the lump of flesh. Whether male or female, all are capable of cultivation; whether layperson or monk, all have their share.
Seek a path to life with urgency, and contemplate the body after this body; by all means, do not rely on returning to your original state.

A dream within a dream. If you wait for tomorrow again and again, look at how you will let your youth go to waste, causing future generations to mourn those who came before, and piling up white bones one after another. Recite the name of Amitābha well;
do not let that golden terrace in his land remain empty. Lord Yama is heartless; do not provoke his iron staff. Abandon evil and follow good; reform your past and cultivate your future.
To the multitude, he proclaimed it for the great assembly; to individual households, he explained it for each family, so that everyone everywhere might simultaneously attain knowledge and awakening.

He taught people so they might all together escape the depths of samsara. If one does not believe the words of the Buddha, what words can be believed? If one does not cultivate the Way, how can one speak of the human path?
He said, "The Way is difficult to cultivate. Each of you must directly take it up; do not let this life pass in vain.

The obstruction of principle is even more severe than that of desire, like a blind man who does not recognize an elephant. There was once a king who gathered a group of blind men and asked them: "You all..."

He wished to know whether they could discern the form of the elephant. They all replied, "We wish to know. He then ordered an elephant handler to lead the elephant into the courtyard and summoned the group of blind men to feel it with their hands.
Once they had finished feeling it, he asked, "Have you now understood the form of the elephant? They all replied, "We have understood."
Thereupon, each made their own estimation. He who felt its trunk said, "The elephant's shape is like a lute. He who felt its legs said, "The elephant's shape is like a pillar.
He who felt its back said, "The elephant's shape is like a house. He who felt its flanks said, "The elephant's shape is like a wall.
He who felt its ears said, "The elephant's shape is like a winnowing basket. He who felt its tail said, "The elephant's shape is like a broom. Thus they spoke, each [according to what he touched].
Each adhered to their own interpretation, arguing without ceasing until they came to blows. The king laughed and said, "None of you truly know the elephant.
The lute is its trunk; the pillars are its feet; the roof is its back; and the walls are its flanks."
The winnowing basket was its ears; the broom was its tail. Consequently, the group of blind men remained silent and did not dare speak.
Yet, in their minds, they still believed what they had felt by touch was not erroneous, and they harbored great resentment toward the other accounts as being entirely wrong.

Thus, throughout their lives, these blind men never truly knew the form of the elephant. Had they not been instructed to feel it with their hands, the shape of the elephant would have remained a matter of mere words.

One should know this: why would one go so far as to engage in contention? It is because they have grasped this once, and thus claim to have personally verified it with their own hands, leaving them utterly free of doubt; consequently, they hold fast to it within and cannot be uprooted.
As for those who do not read the scriptures, if one teaches them to cultivate the Pure Land, even if they do not all come to believe it, they will at least never resort to slander. If...
As soon as one reads the books for the civil service examinations, they immediately consider themselves to be right.

With empty stomachs and haughty minds, they regard this [Buddhism] as nothing more than the teaching of the Buddha, and thus treat its sincere words as absurdities; they view the administration of sweet nectar as if it were lethal poison.
Therefore it is said: "The obstruction of intellectual reasoning is even more severe than that of desire."
First, one must understand the doctrine of the three periods of time.
There are those among scholars who do not believe in past and future lives; because of this, they do not believe in the Pure Land.

This is because they do not realize that past and future lives are simply yesterday and tomorrow—they exist inherently from the very beginning and were not fabricated by the Buddhists. For example: [text continues]
The five viscera and six bowels originally reside within the patient’s own abdomen;

how can it be that because they have emerged from the mouths of physicians, one consequently regards them as mere items in a medicine chest? In the "Exhortation to Students" by Emperor Wenchang, he says at the very outset:
"I have been a scholar-official for seventeen lifetimes. This clearly indicates that there are three lifetimes [within those seventeen].
The titles and honors of the scholar-officials have all passed through his administration; how could his words not be worthy of trust?
Furthermore, one must clarify the principle of cause and effect.
That Confucian scholars do not believe in cause and effect is not a lack of faith in Buddhism, but rather a lack of faith in Confucianism itself. The *I Ching* says: "Accumulation..."
In the house of those who do good, there will surely be an abundance of blessings. In the house of those who accumulate non-good, there will surely be an abundance of calamities.
The Book says: "For doing good, a hundred auspicious signs descend upon them; for doing non-good, a hundred calamities descend upon them. Now, doing good and doing non-good are the causes;
the descent of auspicious signs and the descent of calamities are the effects. It is like the sun and its solar radiance being one and the same thing. Therefore it is said: "If you wish to know..."
"What was caused in a previous life is what one receives in this life. If people believe this teaching, they will naturally dare not commit evil.
Should one regard retribution as absurd, one falls into the state of deceiving and defrauding others without any restraint.
Furthermore, within a single district, if one person believes it and performs one good deed, ten thousand people will increase their store of ten thousand good deeds. One...
If one person does not believe and commits a single evil, ten thousand people will increase their evils by ten thousand. Therefore it is said:
for every person to believe in cause and effect is the way to great order; for every person to disbelieve in cause and effect is the way to great chaos.
The principle of the three periods of time must have been spoken of by Confucius;
the doctrine of the three periods is attested in the classics and histories, where it is recorded in great abundance. Even the events witnessed and heard of in the world today are not few.
Yet, Confucian scholars merely refrain from speaking of it because Confucius never explicitly mentioned it. However, [this is not a reason for its dismissal].
How could there be anything that Confucius did not speak? If it were said that Confucius was ignorant of the three periods of time, he could not be considered a sage.
Within the entire *Lunyu*, the words spoken by Confucius amount to no more than eight thousand five hundred and three characters;
thus, what he spoke but was not transmitted to posterity must be many. If one must wait for it to appear in the canonical scriptures...
If one later believes this, then within the Four Books and Five Classics, Confucius never spoke of his own parents;
a Confucian should likewise conceal and avoid mentioning his own progenitor, just as he never spoke of his own brothers, so that a Confucian should not speak of his siblings,
nor did he ever speak of his houses or fields, so that a Confucian should not dwell in palatial residences or engage in worldly occupations.
"Permanent property. Not only are these the 'Four Treasures of the Study,' for they are not even mentioned in the classics. Your practice of calligraphy is somewhat off the mark.
Beyond the rule of wearing hemp in summer and furs in winter, the classics never speak of 'small garments. Could it be that those who wear trousers today are acting contrary to this?
Regarding gold and tin from Jiangnan, a scholar should not employ them; as for pigments and dyes from Western Shu, a scholar..."
One should not paint [this image]. Why? Because Confucius never uttered these words from his own mouth; they are transmitted solely through the scriptures.

Confucius taught people filial piety and fraternal duty, yet the Confucian scholars are unwilling to practice such filial piety and fraternal duty. He taught people loyalty and reciprocity, yet the Confucian scholars—
Yet he was unwilling to practice loyalty and reciprocity. He never encouraged others to gamble, whereas Confucian scholars were prone to such gambling.
He never taught people to do this or that, yet he insisted on doing certain things himself. As for why he did those particular things—what can be said?
To summarize it in a single word: it is simply that one does not reflect.

The wise should not regard themselves as short-lived, for the human person has never truly died. The name "death" is derived from the physical body; for although the physical body—though... [it perishes].

There is change and alteration; yet my nature is fundamentally without change or alteration. It is like a traveler on a long journey who may ride in a boat or sit in a sedan chair, or may gallop on horseback or drive a carriage.
The boat, carriage, sedan chair, and horse are the physical body; that which rides the boat, carriage, sedan chair, and horse is the true nature.
Speaking in terms of the physical body, it does not last more than a hundred years. But as for what I call one's original face, how could it be so?
To abide as long as heaven and earth—when one reflects quietly upon this, what joy it brings!
Those who today do not believe in future lives know only the physical body and are ignorant of the true nature. This is to clearly regard oneself as short-lived.
This too is a mistaken view.

A person of wisdom must not restrict their perception and learning within the mental perspective of a farmer, for such a person does not know the realm of a wealthy man; nor does one within the mental perspective of a wealthy man know that of an emperor.
Regarding their spheres of experience, though they are equally among human beings, there is a vast disparity between them.
How much more so when one proceeds from humanity to the heavens, and further from the heavens to the Buddha-land! People say that those who read books must possess broad见闻 (insight and learning);
yet how little do they know that the more one reads, the narrower one's insight and learning become, because of the firm and unyielding attachment to the words previously ingested.
To pull out one's own ears. For what they have seen and heard does not extend beyond this single land;
they do not know that worlds are infinite in number, nor that suns and moons are likewise inexhaustible in their multitude.

They speak in vain of the primordial people beginning with Pangu, unaware that since the Great King of Universal Equality first established the world at the beginning of the kalpa, it has already reached the present day.
During the ninth minor kalpa, people knew only that this place was called Zhonghua (Central China);
they did not know that within the single continent of Jambudvīpa, there were already sixteen great nations, five hundred medium-sized nations, and one hundred thousand small nations.
They knew only that when a person reached seventy years of age, it was termed "rare old age" (guxi); they did not know that the people at the beginning of the kalpa all [lived much longer].
For eighty-four thousand years, they knew only that the source of clothing and food in this world must come from agriculture and weaving;

they did not know that in the celestial palaces and Buddha-lands, garments arrive through the mere thought of clothing, and food arrives through the mere thought of food—knowing only gold, silver, and precious treasures.
This region is extremely difficult to reach. One does not know that the lands of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions have great earths composed entirely of the seven treasures;

one sees only the written characters of this region, which consist merely of the Six Scripts created by Cang Jie. One is unaware that since the beginning of creation, there have already been sixty-four types of calligraphic styles.
Knowing only the minor classics of the *Zuo Zhuan*, *Guo Yue*, *Shiji*, and *Hanshu*, one then presumes to be an artist of letters.
The pinnacle of the garden of knowledge. One does not know that within the Secret Scriptures in the Lapis Lazuli Casket atop the Universal Radiance Hall, they are piled as high as mountains;
one only knows that the human fleshly body must be formed from the semen and blood of man and woman.

One does not know that the physical substance is entrusted to a lotus-womb, born in a place of supreme excellence, fragrance, and purity, such that it need not pass through a woman’s belly. One only knows that one has married a single wife.
A woman who is jaundiced and emaciated will then love, cherish, treasure, and dote upon him, listening only to whatever he says;
how could she know that when a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) reigns, in addition to his precious women (yumnī), there are still twenty thousand exquisite ladies?
As for the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the number of his precious women is reckoned in the tens of billions; for each such precious woman—
Beside him, the Heavenly King spontaneously manifested another body to enjoy his entertainment.
He knew only that man is the most intelligent among all things, capable of assisting in the transformation and nourishment of the world, and participating in the workings of Heaven and Earth.

He did not know that the human race is but one path among the six paths of existence, one birth among the four modes of birth, and one realm among the ten realms of reality; he knew only to serve and obtain a single rank or two.

Having attained the rank of a sage, one then claims that their own honor is without equal, asserting that all other gods, spirits, humans, and ghosts are unworthy of belief, and that all matters never personally witnessed are merely absurdities.
How could such a person know that within every land there are many sages presiding over and teaching the transformation of beings? Among the vast multitude of humanity within Jambudvīpa...
There are six thousand four hundred kinds [of beings]. It is not that sages exist only in this single place. Alas!
As for such realms, how could those who pursue sound, form, wealth, and profit ever perceive even a fraction of them?

They are like earthworms, who know only the pleasure of eating mud within a span of a foot of soil, yet remain unaware of the great dragon leaping in the vast ocean amidst surging waves and crashing billows.

It is like a dung beetle, which knows only the pleasure of rolling balls of filth within the manure, yet does not know that the great Peng bird soars ninety thousand li upon the winds that blow below it.
Therefore, those who study the Buddha must truly open their eyes wide.
The Tripitaka must not fail to be read.
Chickens, dogs, oxen, and sheep can crow, bark, bellow, and low, yet they cannot speak; compared to those who are able to speak, those who can speak are truly noble.
A person who does not recognize a single character may be able to speak with their mouth, but they cannot speak with their hands.
Regarding speech, one who has mastered even a few characters can use the pen to communicate across a distance of a thousand *li*; thus, one who has mastered even a few characters is precious.

Although one who has mastered a few characters can use their hand to act as their mouth, they can never transform one hand into a hundred or a thousand hands, nor can they preserve that hand for hundreds or thousands of years. If, however, one could... [be extensive]... then it would be truly marvelous.

One who masters both the ancient and the modern, and composes works to bequeath to posterity, can cause a single book to print hundreds or thousands of others, and allow that single book to endure for hundreds or thousands of years.
Is such a person not most noble? Nevertheless, this is still merely the writing of the mundane world.
If, beyond the Confucian classics, one can further read extensively from the Buddhist canon, then throughout all the heavens above and the earth below, across past kalpas and future...
The kalpas, as well as the dragon palaces and the oceanic treasuries, can all be roughly understood; is what you have seen and heard not already extensive?
Nevertheless, though your learning is indeed vast, if you do not obtain the method of the shortcut to transcend the three realms, then you will still have no share in the seeds of Bodhi.
However, if you can master the Tripitaka and further encounter the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, and are able to practice it with earnest devotion—
Believe in them and practice them accordingly; this is the source from which merit and wisdom arise, and it is not a matter of merely three or five lifetimes.
Someone might say: "Though the texts of the Dragon Palace and the Ocean Treasury are the sincere words of the Tathāgata, what can be done about the fact that Confucian scholars do not believe them?
I reply: Suppose one were to inform them of the deeds of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu.
Those who are illiterate would likewise consider this preposterous; therefore, Buddhist scriptures truly must be read.
Master Xuanzang was exceptionally skilled at providing such inspiration.
In the secular world, some may disparage the Sangha for lacking virtuous conduct and thus fail to believe in the Pure Land; this is an error.
It is like a base Daoist who, because of his own unworthiness, disparages Laozi, or a base scholar who, because of his own unworthiness, disparages Confucius.
A wise person does not reject the words [of a teacher] merely because of the person; how much less could one disparage their teaching because of its followers? As the Tang Emperor Taizong once said:
Dharma Master Xuanzang said, "Your Majesty wishes to provide a vegetarian feast for the Sangha, yet you hear that many monks lack virtuous conduct; what can be done about this?
The Dharma Master replied, "In the Kun Mountains there is jade, yet it is mixed with silt and sand. In the waters of Li there is gold, yet how could there not be shards and rubble?

When clay and wood are carved into Arhats, one receives blessings by honoring them; when copper and iron are cast into golden countenances, one incurs sin by destroying them. It is the same with mud."
"Although a dragon cannot bring rain, one must pray to a clay dragon when seeking rain. Although an ordinary monk cannot bestow blessings, one must revere an ordinary monk when cultivating merit.
Emperor Taizong said with sudden realization, "From this day forward, even if I see a young novice monk..."
It was as if he were honoring the Buddha. Alas! Emperor Taizong truly possessed the merit of past lives; with a single nudge, he was awakened.
One may also say that Master Xuanzang was skilled at providing inspiration.
One should cultivate a mind of weary detachment toward this physical body.
While a person lives in this world, they are tormented by the eight sufferings; yet, unaware of their own suffering, they instead regard it as pleasure.
It is only right that they enter from suffering into further suffering, with no end in sight. To speak of the suffering of birth: while a person dwells within the mother’s womb...
Below the liver and diaphragm, above the large intestine, it forms from the fetal membranes like a bubble, gradually taking shape. Enclosed within the womb, it cannot move freely.
When the mother eats hot food, it is as if she were pouring boiling water over it; when she drinks cold water, it is as if she were lying upon ice.
The place where they dwell is utterly impure; that which they consume consists entirely of unclean blood.

Their stay within the womb does not exceed three hundred days, yet the suffering they endure is equivalent to many decades. Upon reaching full term, their bodies are inverted and suspended with the head toward the birth canal.
As their physical form gradually grows larger, they have no means of exit; the path to their own destruction lies in this very state.

It is carved; the mechanism for killing the mother is also contained within this single moment. At this time, the mother pulls it from the womb, and the pain is as if she were being torn apart by chariots.
Therefore, once it emerges from the womb, there is no one who does not let out a loud cry. After emerging from the womb, urine and excrement are scattered in disarray.
They do not know shame. It is the same with those who are called the great wealthy and the highly noble; it is the same with those who are called the great sages and the great worthies.
People merely habituate themselves to these things as if they were natural, and thus remain unaware and unconscious of them.

If one could reflect upon this for a single clear night, would it not be a source of sorrow and shame? The Tathāgata, the Great Sage, out of compassion for the world, teaches people to seek rebirth [in the Pure Land].

In the Pure Land, one is born by transformation from a lotus flower, thereby escaping such calamities and hardships. Yet, alas, you remain addicted and immersed in defilement, failing to give rise to thoughts of weary detachment.
A person of great filial piety does not wish to enter a womb.
When the divine consciousness enters the womb, not only does the individual suffer, but the mother likewise undergoes immense agony.

Throughout the ten months in the womb, each day passes as if it were a year. Upon reaching the moment of birth, the mother’s suffering takes myriad forms, so profound that it is difficult to describe.
Moment by moment she dwells as if beside ghosts; in every thought she longs for life yet cannot find it. Fortunately, this ordeal...
Life passes by in haste. One then cherishes an infant as if it were a treasure; for this reason, one pushes aside the dry bedding to lie upon the damp, caring for and supporting them.
Thus, throughout one's life, much of one’s vital essence and blood is consumed in secret. Long ago, there was a seven-year-old śrāmaṇera who left the household life and attained the Way.
He recalled his own past lives and sighed, saying: "My single body has caused five mothers to suffer in grief.

When I was the son of my first mother, a neighbor’s child was born at the same time; I alone died young, and when my mother saw that neighbor’s child grow up, she immediately gave rise to sorrow and distress.
When I was the son of my second mother, I again died prematurely; if my mother saw someone nursing a child, she would immediately give rise to grief."
As for the third time he was my son, he died at the age of ten; when my mother saw other children eating and drinking like myself, she immediately gave rise to grief and distress.
As for the fourth time he was my son, he died before marriage; when my mother saw his peers taking wives, she immediately gave rise to grief and distress.
Now we are in the fifth lifetime: he left home at the age of seven, and as my mother remembers him, she again gives rise to grief and distress.
I reflect upon the cycle of birth and death; my accumulated kin have been like this. This is why I am moved by emotion to advance in the Way of cultivation.

Today, on the streets, people shoulder to shoulder and heel to heel pass by without ceasing; yet for the most part, those who leave a burden upon their parents are many, while those who can repay their parental kindness are but few.
To be conceived in the womb for a single lifetime already burdens one’s parents; if one were to be so conceived a hundred times—
To leave behind one’s parents for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas is a burden;
if one can transcend the mundane world and be born through transformation within a lotus flower, one will never again burden one’s parents—is this not the greatest of great filial piety?
Yet those who slander the Buddha today claim instead that leaving home is unfilial; they are those who would rather willingly remain in the womb, thereby burdening their parents.
This is what it means to be a true relative.
Great nobles should know to feel self-reproach;
for those called "noble" are not defined by the dignity of their rank or the prominence of their station, nor by the mastery of the five carts of learning. It refers rather to one who is able—
"To depart from" refers to base behaviors. This means being able to abandon those base behaviors common to beasts and birds.

Wherein does this baseness lie? It is said to be greed, lust, killing, and theft; these are what they share with birds and beasts. Beyond these, there remains something even more shameful and loathsome:
namely, the matter of digesting excrement within the belly. This is true regardless of whether the food consists of rare delicacies or a hundred flavors.
Once it enters the throat, it becomes one with the saliva, spittle, and brain-phlegm, flowing down along with them.

Within the stomach, there are yellowish long-worms that contract, extend, and writhe inside; after a full day and night, they bore into and gnaw at it for digestion, flowing into the large intestine until its stench is unbearable to approach.
As these accumulate in great quantities, they eventually gush forth through both the large and small excretory paths, appearing loathsome and foul.
Its appearance is like that of a dog or a pig. This kind of base behavior, even if committed but once, is already shameful; how can one endure it daily?
If one possesses such base conduct yet remains unaware of it and seeks no renunciation, one is no different from birds and beasts.
Therefore, one must surely reproach oneself and repent, desiring to cast off this state at every moment; only then will this base condition become truly noble.
Among these beings of the six heavens, although they consume the heavenly *sudhā* nectar, it is fragrant, pure, light, and clear, devoid of even the slightest speck of dust or dross.
Fragrant clouds well forth from their bodies with sovereign ease. They travel instantaneously across hundreds of thousands of millions of lands;

they are free from tears, phlegm, saliva, and the impurities of excrement and urine. Therefore, the nails and claws of these celestial beings are worth more than those of [the inhabitants of] Yama’s realm.
Although one may dwell upon the land of Jambudvīpa, one cannot be called a person of great nobility so long as one remains subject to the cycle of saṃsāra.
It is only by transcending the mundane world and being born through transformation within a lotus flower that this state of lowliness can be forever severed.
This is not something that the power of Confucius or Mencius can save me from.

The metaphor of the silkworm cocoon refers to the silkworm’s making of its cocoon. Having already spun it to the left and the right, above and below, it exhausts everything within its belly to complete it;
only then does it suppose itself to dwell permanently therein, secure and unharmed. How could it know why this is so?
For those who manage their own affairs and pursue their own interests, is this not precisely what entangles and binds them?

How could they know that others rely on what they have spat out to protect themselves, while people use what they have spat out to destroy themselves? There are tens of thousands, even millions, of such deluded creatures.
Who can escape the boiling cauldron? Yet, in that place, the father transmits it to the son, and the son transmits it to the grandson, entering the boiling cauldron;
thus, nothing is more miserable than this. It is like a cocoon within the two great gates of the world.
It is exactly like this. Exhausting a lifetime of toil, they strive solely to provide food and clothing for their wives and children;
they employ all manner of stratagems and harbor enmities, leaving no means untried. By the time their household affairs are roughly established, their own bodies are already bound within them.
Among the tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of deluded people, who can escape the cycle of retribution? Yet they continue to bring forth children...
Furthermore, it is transmitted from son to grandson, and from grandson to great-grandson, as a form of retribution. Thus, nothing is more extraordinary than this.
As the *Sutra in Forty-two Sections* says: "A person's attachment to wife, children, and home is worse than being in prison;
for while there is a time when one may be released from prison, there is no thought of ever being parted from one's wife and children."
The metaphor of the basket is as follows: a fisherman sets a basket in midstream to prevent fish from passing through.

He floats water plants alongside it to give the appearance that it is a place of concealment, while secretly burying beneath the grass a basket that can be entered but not exited. Thereupon, the fish—
They scramble to cast themselves into it, thinking it a place where they may find refuge and rest, unaware that they have already entered the basket.

It is just so with the fishing nets and curtains within the River of Desire. People only think that as long as they are free from illness and suffering, their homes are secure and their wives and children can be relied upon;
thus they pass their time aimlessly and heedlessly, neither perceiving nor realizing it. Suddenly, the basket of Old Yama rises up. And...
Those whom one most cherishes—father and son, husband and wife—are each recorded in their registers and summoned away.
To contemplate this, how could it not be lamentable? Yet mere lamentation is of no avail; the only superior strategy is to ensure that they do not dare to summon them.
Regarding the parable of the horse, there are four types. The most excellent and noble horse gallops at the mere sight of the shadow of the whip, without waiting for being spurred.

Next is that which runs as soon as it is struck once by the whip. Further down is that which does not run when the whip strikes lightly, but only runs when the whip strikes heavily. And finally, there is the lowest type, the dull-witted horse.
Even with heavy lashes, one does not run away; it is only when the awl pierces the skin and the pain becomes extreme that one finally flees.
Human beings are likewise: those who possess wisdom awaken easily. Upon hearing of someone's death within a hundred *li*, one should immediately be struck with alarm, thinking:
"Within a hundred *li* there is one who has died; I too am a human being, and death will surely reach me. One must then practice with urgency to seek liberation.
This refers to those who gallop upon seeing the shadow of the whip. The next class awakens upon seeing a close relative die.

Even further down are those who awaken only after seeing a neighbor die. If one waits until one’s own old age or until one is personally ill before awakening, one is already like someone who runs only after the needle has pierced the skin. Should one still not awaken even when old...
Awakening. Or, having already fallen ill, one still does not awaken; is this not equivalent to being even worse than the wild fox?
The parable of the wild fox tells of a wild fox that enters the kitchen at night, eats its fill, and falls asleep. When dawn breaks, unable to escape, it feigns death.
Yet it waited for others to abandon it; before long, there was indeed one who wished to discard it. One person said, "The fox's tail is quite fine;
I shall wait until I have cut it off before discarding you. Upon hearing this, the fox was terrified; enduring the pain, it allowed itself to be cut.
Suddenly, a young boy arrived, wishing to take its two ears. Hearing this, the fox became even more afraid, yet it reflected that the two ears were still unrelated to its essential nature.
He continued to endure it. Shortly thereafter, another person said, "The fur can be used to patch a robe.
The fox was greatly terrified and said, "If they take my skin, they will surely cut off my head and rip open my belly; how can this be endured?
Thereupon, he sprang up and fled wildly toward the outside, and the fox eventually escaped. Humans within the prison of the three realms are no different from being in a kitchen. Karma—
Once one has been entrusted with a womb and become human, it is already difficult to escape the certainty of death.
Only by reciting the Buddha’s name to attain rebirth in the Pure Land can one escape from the jaws of death. Having missed the time of physical vigor, the fox-tail has already been cut off;

if one reaches the twilight years of the "sanguyu" period, it will be as if one's head is about to be severed or one's belly ripped open. Unless one establishes a great vow and exerts oneself regardless of one's own life, how could one possibly succeed?
"Will one leap out of the path of delusion and receive the guidance of the Buddha?

To blame it all upon the Lord of the Netherworld alone—when one dies and appears before the Lord of the Netherworld, they must undergo punishment according to their karma. The person said, "If I had known this earlier, Great King, why..."
"Before this, did you not first pass through a single message? The King of the Underworld said, "You have indeed passed through them. That your hair gradually turned yellow was the first message.
That your teeth gradually became loose was the second message. That your strength gradually declined was the third message.
That your ears and eyes gradually grew dim and deaf was the fourth and fifth messages. These messages have been delivered to you many times. Yet here is a young man who weeps."
He replied, "I have attained faith, yet I am not yet fully enlightened. The King of the Netherworld said, "Your attainments are indeed many.
Do you still remember that certain youth who died of illness and perished from the plague? That certain youth who was wounded by a blade and died by hanging?
That certain youth who drowned in water, was consumed by fire, devoured by a wolf, or stung by a snake? All these were instances of your faith. How could this be otherwise?"

One must certainly call out one's name and announce it. Even if you possess the courage to uproot mountains and surpass the world, or the talent to overturn heaven and turn over the earth, can you escape the interrogations here?

Only by remaining transcendent beyond worldly affairs can one not only avoid these interrogations, but even cause the King of the Netherworld to revere and pay homage to you; that is, through the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
Regarding those who attain rebirth:
when a moth flutters into a lamp and dies, it does not die because of the oil or the fire; it dies because of its perception. So it is with humans.
If one pities them and drives them away, they will surely seize the opportunity to throw themselves [into it].
Thinking that what I have perceived must not be erroneous, they press forward without hesitation until death. This is because people crave sound and beauty, and crave wealth and profit.
As for those who are addicted to gambling, their vision likewise extends no further than this;
thus they rush headlong forward until death brings them to a halt. Why not take the moth as a lesson?

Regarding the fly’s delusion within the window: when a fly is at a window, it circles and hovers back and forth, unable to exit for the entire day because it is constrained by what it perceives and cannot take a single step back.
If it could suddenly take that one step back, everywhere would be open.
The ocean is vast and the sky is wide. This Sahā world is like a great window-pane;

from antiquity until now, who knows how many deluded flies have been shut inside it? Fortunately, I have now suddenly taken a step back and am flying toward the West. I fly toward the West! How joyful!
Regarding the four methods for training horses:
In the time of the Buddha, there was a skilled trainer of fine steeds. The Buddha asked him how many methods he employed. He replied that he used four methods: first, kindness; second, severity;
third, severity followed by kindness; and fourth, kindness followed by severity. The Buddha said, "Those four methods do not truly train [the mind]. He then led [the discussion further].
"What should be done? The Master of Horses replied, "One should simply kill it. "When the World-Honored One teaches and transforms sentient beings, what methods should he employ?
The Buddha said, "He likewise employs four methods. The first is the use of kindness, which refers to those who possess good faith;
they are taught to practice and study the Way. The second is the use of awe, which refers to those who commit evil; they are shown the revolving cycle of the three miserable realms. The third is..."
"First, he teaches them by means of practicing the Way; fourthly, he first shows them the cycle of rebirth within the three miserable realms.
Master Ma asked, "If these four methods fail to transform them, what shall we do? The Buddha said, "I shall also kill them. Master Ma said, "The Tathāgata possesses great compassion."

"Why did he carry out the killing? The Buddha said, "The four dharmas could not transform him; even instruction was of no benefit. He then ceased speaking with him, and because he did not speak with him, [the king] killed him.

Regarding the Eye Medicine: when the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Queen Māyā (the consort of King Śuddhodana), while in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, experienced several types of evil dreams.
Among them was one dream in which she saw the sun disk suddenly set in the lower realm, leaving the entire world in darkness.
There were countless rākṣasas holding sharp knives in their hands, gouging out the eyes of the people of the world.
Māyā sighed and said, "This must surely be an omen that my son, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, will enter nirvāṇa. Shortly thereafter, the Venerable Aniruddha—
Indeed, he has ascended to heaven to deliver this report. Those books in the world that slander the Triple Gem are all those that gouge out the eyes of people.
As the merit-power of people in the final age becomes increasingly shallow, such books become more numerous;
as their wisdom becomes increasingly feeble, those who revere such books become more numerous. Therefore, those with merit must act early.
To awaken for oneself and not be pierced by it is truly the highest state.
Should one nevertheless be wounded by it, one should quickly apply a wondrous medicine. What is this medicine? Scripture is one such means.
There is a vow that will surely be fulfilled:
Lord Lü Wenzheng of the Song Dynasty, whose courtesy name was Shengong. During the reign of Emperor Taizong, he ranked first in the jinshi examinations and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Xu.
Every morning when he arose to pay homage to the Buddha, he would invariably offer this prayer: "May those who do not believe in the Buddha not be born into my family. May it be so.
My descendants have enjoyed the imperial bounty for generations and have protected and upheld the Triple Gem. Later, my son Yijian was enfeoffed as the Duke of Shen;
every New Year’s Day, after performing his prostrations at the family shrine, he would immediately pay his respects to Chan Master Guanghui.
Yijian’s son, Gongzhu, was also enfeoffed as the Duke of Shen, and he treated Chan Master Tianyi in the same manner. Hao Wen, the Vice President of the Left, [treated] Chan Master Yuan...
Master Fozhao was also like this. Yongzhong, the son of the Vice President of the Left, was likewise so toward Master Fozhao.

Their lineages have been noble and prominent for generations, fulfilling the vows of Master Foguo Fuyu. Now, what Wen Zheng expected was merely a worldly aspiration, yet he was still able to achieve it;
how much more so for one who has resolved to attain Bodhicitta and vows to be reborn in An-yang—how could such a person not succeed in their quest?
One who is a member of the Sangha must not fail to cultivate the Pure Land.
The Chan Master Qingcaotang of the Song dynasty was always possessed of pure preceptual conduct; he was over ninety years of age, and the Zeng family constantly provided for his sustenance.
He repeatedly bestowed clothing and other goods upon the Sangha, who, moved by his virtue, granted him permission to be reborn into his family.

Later, when the wife of the Zeng clan gave birth to a son, she sent someone to check on the thatched hall; he was already sitting in meditation at the moment of passing away. The son born to her was none other than Zeng Gong (Zeng Xi).

Because he had cultivated merit and wisdom in a previous life, he achieved high rank in the civil service at a young age and later served as a worthy prime minister. This is also like the case of [the monk] at the end of the Ming dynasty...
A monk named Da Cheng from Zhejiang was collecting leftover rice from alms bowls to provide for the assembly at his temple.
On his way, he passed by the home of the Shi family, who were devoted Buddhists; whenever a monk came to beg for food, they would invariably invite him to stay.

After Da Cheng collected the rice and returned to the temple, the Shi family noticed that his daily portion was small, so they would regularly supplement it with their own rice until it was full. The Shi family had long been childless, but later their wife suddenly became pregnant. They divided [the merit].
At the time of delivery, Chengda personally saw him enter the bedroom. He hurriedly pursued him and questioned him, but Chengda was nowhere to be found;

yet the woman eventually gave birth to a son. On that day, Chengda did not come to receive his meal. When the temple administrator went to inquire after him, he learned that Chengda had passed away on that very day.
Consequently, the child was named Chengda. In his early childhood, the boy was exceptionally intelligent.
Xiaoyou observed the *ruci* fast while in the womb and maintained his precepts without violation throughout his life.
In the year Yiwu of the Shunzhi era, he became the grand champion of the empire. From a secular perspective, these two gentlemen were both wealthy, noble, and enjoyed great fame.
However, from the perspective of a practitioner of the Way, both monks made many errors. Had the two masters known the Dharma-gate of the Western Land...
As for those who practice, they dedicate their merit toward the Pure Land. Even if one cannot attain the highest grade, one may still achieve the middle grade;
why limit oneself to merely becoming a top scholar or a prime minister?
High monks should also cultivate the Pure Land.

Shi Xuanjing of Xiangzhou during the Sui dynasty was proficient in both the doctrinal and practical aspects of the teachings, and his reputation for the Way spread far and wide. In the sixth month of the second year of the Daye era, he...

As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he bathed and sat upright. With his two eyes gazing upward, he suddenly said of himself, "I wish to be born in the Tuṣita Inner Court to see Maitreya Bodhisattva;
why then have I become the King of the Yama Heaven? When the assembly questioned him about this, he replied:
"This is not something you can understand. Shortly thereafter, he further remarked, "It is very busy in heaven; there are so many guests," and then he passed away while sitting upright. Alas!
When the Master was practicing his cultivation, he certainly resolved to see Maitreya; yet, upon reaching this point, he was unable to see him.
He has even been reborn as a celestial king. From a worldly perspective, his status is already above that of the Supreme Deity (Shangdi).
Yet, when compared to those born in the Western Land [of Ultimate Bliss], he falls far short. Thus, we know that even eminent monks must cultivate the Pure Land.
One must not accept with complacency the fate of becoming a ghost.

Among all human beings in the great trichiliocosm—regardless of their status as noble or lowly, wise or foolish, old or young, male or female—once they have reached the end of life, if they do not emerge into the world [of rebirth], there are none who will not become ghosts. Therefore, I exhort people to recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
This is an exhortation to worldly people not to become ghosts. Lesser Confucians do not believe in the Buddha-dharma and instead proceed to slander it;
not only do they willingly accept becoming ghosts themselves, but they also seek to urge all worldly people to become ghosts.
Those among them who are not ghosts at present are merely so for the time being. At this very moment, all these countless people will, in the blink of an eye—
The Forest of the Afterlife: This forest comprises all manner of ghosts. Humans alone do not realize that life is exceedingly brief;

thus, they exhaust their bodies and weary their spirits in pursuit of wealth and honor. Let alone whether they attain such wealth and honor, even if one reaches the pinnacle of riches and nobility, at the moment of departure, one cannot carry a single coin in hand.
A single ghost calls out and one must immediately depart; what, then, is the point of it?
Is it not wealth and honor? Yet for one who alone practices mindfulness of the Buddha, upon reaching this point, they pass away peacefully and without illness or calamity;
their body is free from all suffering, disease, and misfortune, and their mind is free from all greed, attachment, and delusion. When evil spirits behold their shadow, they vanish;
when the Lord of Yama hears their name, he bows his head in reverence. Are these not truly great men who have transcended the world? It is only through human effort that...
Only after this can one finally avoid becoming a ghost. Thus, not becoming a ghost is truly not easy.

As for those of the nine classes who should all attain rebirth, these nine classes are: namely, womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, transformation-born; with form, without form; with perception, without perception; [and so forth].

It is neither with perception nor without perception. These nine categories encompass all things from the noble and the lowly to the hidden and the manifest, as well as the entire range of the heavens above and the earth below.
Within these nine categories, the most suffering are the three evil realms; the most joyful are the twenty-eight heavens of the triple world.
This is solely because one has not yet transcended birth and death, and thus wanders in saṃsāra through the six paths. As for those who suffer, it is certainly...
Suffering. Even pleasure is suffering. Although the devas of long life currently enjoy boundless bliss, when their heavenly merit is exhausted, they still fall into the three miserable realms.
How can this compare to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where one is forever liberated from saṃsāra and bids eternal farewell to the six destinies?
I have formerly burned incense and prostrated myself in the temples of Wenchang, the God of War, and the East Peak.

Afterwards, he would invariably offer this prayer: "May the Imperial Lord honor and believe in the Triple Gem, resolve to attain Bodhicitta, be reborn in the Western Paradise, and practice the path of the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, whenever he prostrated before the Honored Mother of the Stars (Doubumu) and the Supreme God of Heaven (Haotian Shangdi), even after his expressions of utmost sincerity and awe—bowing his head to the ground and striking it repeatedly—he likewise prayed that the Most Honorable One might practice mindfulness of the Buddha, be reborn in the Pure Land, and cultivate the path of the Bodhisattva. Extensively...
It delivers all beings. Why is this? It is simply because those with wisdom perceive that among the most sublime and lofty matters in the world, none surpasses the recitation of the Buddha's name;
and among the most meritorious deeds, none equals rebirth in the Pure Land.
Reciting the Buddha’s name and attaining rebirth is beyond comparison with any other form of merit. The Honored Celestial Mother is, in fact, the Bodhisattva Mārīcī mentioned in the sutras.
The Great Heaven God (Hao Tian Shang Di) is none other than the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven mentioned in the sutras.

Whenever the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven never fails to pay respectful homage and stands in attendance at his side. Hearing this silent prayer today, he will surely rejoice;
there is absolutely no possibility that he would instead bring about misfortune or transgression. It is our good fortune to have encountered this Dharma door. Not...
One who contemplates with courageous diligence and dedicates [the merit] toward Bodhi— is this not indeed what the Tathāgata calls most worthy of compassion?
One should recollect the Buddha’s power that is never exerted in vain.
In worldly affairs, if a plan fails to succeed, all prior effort is cast away.

Only in the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is it the case that even if one begins but does not complete the practice, what has been recited in the past will never have been in vain. Long ago, there was a woodcutter who encountered a tiger and climbed a tree.

If merely reciting "Namo Buddha" once leads one to rely upon it for renunciation and gradually attain Buddhahood after many births and kalpas, how much more so for those who practice with sincerity throughout their entire lives?
Even if one cannot achieve rebirth in the Pure Land in this present life, one will certainly transcend birth and death in a future existence.
This is not like worldly scholars who fail in their studies and waste their spirit, or those who fail in their business ventures and instead suffer in vain.
This means to lose one's capital.
Among the superior matters of the human world, none compare to the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation).
The *Piyu jing* (Sutra of Similes) says: "In the past, there was a husband and wife who prayed to Heaven for a child. The wife then became pregnant and gave birth to four [sons]."
There were four kinds of objects: first, a *droṇa* measure of sandalwood rice; second, a jar of nectar-like honey; third, a precious jewel-embroidered bag;
and fourth, a seven-jointed divine staff. The man sighed and said, "I originally sought a son; what use have I for these objects? The deity asked, "Why do you desire a son?
The man replied, "I desire a son so that I may bring him home and hope he will provide me with support. The deity [said]:...
He said: "The rice within the measure-dipper becomes full again as soon as it is taken; the jar of sweet dew can eliminate a hundred ailments; the pouch of precious jewels is inexhaustible when used;
and the seven-jointed divine staff is prepared to ward off violence. How could a filial son among men achieve such things?
The man was greatly delighted and subsequently attained great wealth. Later, other countries heard of this and dispatched troops to seize it. His...
A person carrying a staff flies through the air and strikes back [the enemy], protecting them for the rest of their life.

Among the people of the world, those who are so diligent and frantic that they find no leisure for spiritual practice do so merely for the sake of a wife and children. Yet, even if a wife and children were to serve one with the utmost devotion, how could they ever be like these four objects?
As for attaining rebirth in the Western Paradise, one transcends birth and death and is adorned with myriad blessings—this is what is truly sought.

It is as you wish. Furthermore, how could it possibly be measured by means of the four objects? Therefore, among all things in heaven and on earth, nothing surpasses the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*).
*Qixin zashe* (Miscellaneous Discourses on Arousing Faith) concludes here.
